C005.subject: GDP per capita
C005.predicate: underestimates material living standards in countries with high non-market household production
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: GDP per capita material living standards]

[PATH:empirical] Time-use surveys and satellite accounts on household production (e.g., from the OECD or national statistical offices) comparing GDP per capita with augmented measures of material living standards that include non-market household output. — Directly tests whether the gap between GDP and an inclusive consumption measure is larger in low-income, subsistence-agriculture economies, confirming the hypothesized underestimation.

[PATH:empirical] Cross-country studies of subjective well-being and material deprivation indices (e.g., the Gallup World Poll or the Multidimensional Poverty Index) regressed on GDP per capita and household production proxies. — If GDP per capita is a poorer predictor of self-reported material living standards in high non-market production contexts, that would confirm the hypothesis; if not, it would refute it.

[PATH:literature] Theoretical literature on the 'GDP paradox' and the 'beyond GDP' movement, particularly papers by Nordhaus, Stiglitz, and Sen (e.g., the 2009 Stiglitz-Sen-Fitoussi Commission report). — Provides foundational arguments and proposed measurement frameworks that directly address the systematic bias of GDP in the presence of non-market production, helping to contextualize and refine the hypothesis.

qualifier.geographic: globally, with strongest effect in low-income and subsistence-agriculture economies

C006.subject: GDP per capita
C006.predicate: is not a valid proxy for
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: GDP per capita material living standards]

[PATH:empirical] OECD Better Life Index and national accounts data (e.g., GDP per capita vs. household disposable income, consumption, and non-market indicators) — Directly tests whether GDP per capita correlates with multidimensional material living standards (e.g., housing, income, jobs) across developed economies post-1950, using cross-country and time-series regression.

[PATH:literature] Mismeasuring Our Lives: Why GDP Doesn't Add Up (Stiglitz, Sen, Fitoussi, 2010) and subsequent UN/World Bank reports on Beyond GDP metrics — Provides theoretical and empirical critiques of GDP as a welfare proxy, including alternative composite indices (e.g., HDI, SPI) that can be compared against GDP per capita to assess validity.

[PATH:empirical] Panel data analysis of subjective well-being (e.g., World Happiness Report, Eurobarometer) vs. GDP per capita in developed economies — Tests if changes in GDP per capita track changes in self-reported material satisfaction, controlling for inequality, public goods, and non-market production, thus directly addressing the proxy claim.

C007.subject: GDP per capita
C007.object: subjective wellbeing and social cohesion in post-industrial economies
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: GDP per capita subjective wellbeing and social cohesion in post-industrial economies]

[PATH:empirical] OECD Better Life Index and World Values Survey longitudinal data (2008-2023) — Cross-national panel analysis of GDP per capita against life satisfaction and trust indicators can directly test the hypothesized negative correlation in post-industrial economies.

[PATH:literature] Easterlin Paradox updated meta-analysis (e.g., recent work by Easterlin or Bartolini) — Review of updated empirical studies on the Easterlin Paradox focusing on post-industrial OECD countries provides a theoretical and empirical baseline to confirm or refute the negative correlation claim.

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal social cohesion indices (e.g., from the Bertelsmann Transformation Index or European Social Survey) — Time-series data on social cohesion (e.g., social trust, civic participation) paired with GDP per capita trends can isolate the relationship within the specified temporal and geographic scope.

C008.subject: GDP per capita
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: GDP per capita subjective wellbeing and social cohesion]

[PATH:empirical] Easterlin Paradox longitudinal studies (e.g., Easterlin et al., 2010) examining GDP per capita and life satisfaction trends within OECD countries post-2000 — Directly tests the hypothesized positive relationship between GDP per capita and subjective wellbeing, with evidence that beyond a certain threshold, income gains do not correlate with increased happiness, thus challenging the proxy claim.

[PATH:empirical] OECD Better Life Index and Social Cohesion indicators (e.g., trust, inequality, social support) compared against GDP per capita across OECD nations — Provides multi-dimensional data to assess whether GDP per capita strongly correlates with social cohesion measures, or whether other factors (e.g., inequality, institutional quality) mediate the relationship, potentially refuting the hypothesis.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical frameworks from Sen's capabilities approach and Putnam's social capital theory — Argues that wellbeing and cohesion are multidimensional and not reducible to economic output, offering a conceptual basis for why GDP per capita may be a weak proxy, guiding empirical tests of alternative indicators.

[PATH:empirical] OECD Better Life Index (BLI) panel data (2010–2023) with subjective well-being, leisure time, and environmental indicators — Directly tests the predictive power of the composite index vs. GDP per capita for cross-country variation in human wellbeing, using OECD countries as specified.

[PATH:literature] Easterlin Paradox replication studies (e.g., Bartolini, Bilancini, & Sarracino, 2013) on long-term life satisfaction trends and GDP growth — Provides theoretical and empirical evidence on GDP's limitations as a well-being proxy, supporting the hypothesis that composite indicators may be superior.

[PATH:empirical] New Economics Foundation's Happy Planet Index (HPI) time-series analysis (2010–2020) for OECD nations — The HPI combines life satisfaction, life expectancy, and ecological footprint; comparing its correlation with alternative well-being measures against GDP's correlation can refute or confirm the hypothesis.
